## Point 2:

> Describe the **distribution** of `price` and of `log(price)` using the **descriptive statistics** you find appropriate. Comment the results you obtain.

### 2.1 Price Distribution

```{r}
hist(data$price, col = "lightblue", breaks = 75, main = "Histogram of Price",
     xlab = "Price")
```

By looking at the graph it seems that there are **extreme outliers** on the right.

Before continuing with the task of displaying the log graph we will briefly look at the descriptive statistics of `price`, Both from a numerical standpoint and a graphical (we though boxplot would be the best visualization aid)

```{r}
summary(data$price)
```

By looking at the graph we notice 2 things:

- MIN-MAX RANGE is equal of almost 4 .5 million usd -

- MEAN \> MEDIAN which means that there are pretty high values that inflate the mean

In order to understand how many outliers exists that inflate the mean we will now use a boxplot

```{r}
boxplot(data$price, col = "lightblue", horizontal = TRUE,
        main = "Boxplot of Price", xlab = "Price")
```

It is pretty clear that there are many many outliers especially near the third qualntile. It migh be interesting to see wether they have a logical/historical sense

### 2.2 Logaritimc distribution of price

By using a log transformation, we squeeze the larger values more than the smaller ones. Since price has a heavy right tail and a fairly short left tail, we will probably see a roughly symmetric distribution

```{r}
hist(log(data$price), col = "lightblue", breaks = 75, main = "Histogram of Price",
     xlab = "Price")
```

We just proved what we've just said.

### 2.3 Comparison of `price` and `log(price)` Boxplots

It might be interesting to compare this `log(price)` boxplot with the `price` one

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))   # 1 row, 2 plots

boxplot(data$price, col = "lightblue", main = "Price", ylab = "Price")
boxplot(log(data$price), col = "lightgreen", main = "Log(Price)", ylab = "Log(Price)")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))   # reset layout
```

After the logarimic transformation we notice a clearer quartile range, even the median now lies near its center, showing a much more symmetric distribution. As said before for the nature of the log, we partially pulled in the right tail, but streched the left one.So now the very cheap houses will appear as outliers.

Based on the Group Asignment task we will keep the original price for descriptive comparisons; but we'll consider the log transformation later when checking the model assumptions.

## Part 3

> Describe (possibly, with plots) the **relationship** between price and some numerical variables you find more interesting (at least 3), and comment on the most relevant and **meaningful correlations** you find in the data

### 3.0 Chain of thought for the choice of relationship to show

In order to choose the variables to compare with price, we believed it might be a good idea to compute the correlation matrix, as it might come in hand with the next steps.

### 3.1 Pearson Correlation Matrix

As we have 21 features i will plot the corr. matrix of the 10 most correlated features

```{r}
quant_cols = which(sapply(data, is.numeric))
cor_matrix = cor(data[, quant_cols])      

top10 = names(sort(abs(cor_matrix[, "price"]), decreasing = TRUE))[2:11]
cor_top = cor_matrix[c("price", top10), c("price", top10)]

corrplot(cor_top, method = "color", type = "lower",     # type è per decidere se mostarre il triangolo di sopra o sotto
         addCoef.col = "black", number.cex = 0.7,
         tl.col = "black", tl.cex = 0.8, diag = FALSE)

```

Based on this matrix we will look at the relationship beetween `price` and:

- `sqt_living`: {living area}

- `grade`: {construction quality according to the county (1–13)}

- `sqft15`: {average areas of the 15 nearest houses} aka {the quality of the area}

> Although `sqft_above` is the third most correlated variable with price, we chose `sqft_living15` instead. Their correlations with price are almost identical (0.61 vs 0.59), but `sqft_above` is highly correlated with `sqft_living` (0.88, as it is part of the living area), so it adds little new information. `sqft_living15` is less correlated with it (0.76) and captures a different aspect: the size of the neighbouring houses.

### 3.2 Relationship Display

#### `Price`- `sqft_living`

```{r}
# sqft_living
plot(data$sqft_living, data$price, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.3),
     xlab = "sqft_living", ylab = "Price", main = "Price vs sqft_living")
abline(lm(price ~ sqft_living, data = data), col = "red", lwd = 2)

# design choice: 
# cex = 0.5 because if i put 1 then the circles would have covered each other even more as we dealing with many data paoints
# I used rgb as i wanted to insert opacity
```

By looking at this plot the general idea we can take with us is that price and square foot area have a **positive linear relationship**. As the living square foots increase, price follows.

However, one thing to notice is that as \`sqft_living\` increases the spread of price grows with size: small huses have very similar prices, while large houses vary much more wich might be a signal for **heteroschedasticity**

#### `Price`-`grade`

```{r}
# grade
boxplot(price ~ grade, data = data, col = "lightblue",
        xlab = "grade", ylab = "Price", main = "Price by grade")
```

By looking at this graph, we can notice how

- The median price grows positively proportionally with grade (as suggested by the corr.matrix)

- The increase of price is not linear: from grade 3 to 7 prices barely change, while from grade 9 upwards they rise much faster

- The spread of prices grows disproportionately with grade, as shown by the increasing interquartile ranges. This supports our earlier observation of heteroscedasticity.

#### `Price`-`sqft_living15`

```{r}
# sqft_living15
plot(data$sqft_living15, data$price, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.3),
     xlab = "sqft_living15", ylab = "Price", main = "Price vs sqft_living15")
abline(lm(price ~ sqft_living15, data = data), col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

We have a very similar situation to the one we had with sqft_living. So a positive correlation, almost linear with a price range spread that grows with the sqft_living 15 (heteroschedasticity again)

> Commento che ha scritto claude (non da cancellare ma da rivedere -voglio inviarvi il prima possibile il notebook. lo riguardo nel mentre che voi lavorate al resto.
>
> The pattern is very similar to the one with sqft_living: a positive, almost linear relationship (r = 0.59), with a spread of prices that grows with sqft_living15 (heteroscedasticity again). The relationship is weaker, as the points are more scattered around the line. This suggests that the size of the neighbouring houses, a proxy for the quality of the area, is linked to price. However, since sqft_living15 is strongly correlated with sqft_living (r = 0.76), part of this relationship may simply reflect that large houses tend to be located near other large houses

## Part 4

> Use a proper plot to compare price across the levels of waterfront and view. Comment

### 4 Plotting of `waterfront` and `view` with boxplots

Boxplots are the best choice to compare these 2 variables as they represent categorical values.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

boxplot(price ~ waterfront, data = data, log = "y",
        col = c("lightgrey", "lightblue"), names = c("No", "Yes"),
        xlab = "Waterfront", ylab = "Price (log scale)", main = "Price by waterfront")

boxplot(price ~ view, data = data, log = "y",
        col = hcl.colors(5, "Blues", rev = TRUE),
        xlab = "View quality (0–4)", ylab = "Price (log scale)", main = "Price by view")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

> We used a log scale as groups differ greatly in price level, if we used the original distribution it would have been hard to compare the boxes.

By looking at these 2 graphs we can say that:

- Waterfront houses are far more expensive: the interquartile boxes doesn't even overlap.

- Price also increases with view quality, but not evenly

- Both plots shows many outliers, especially among non-waterfront houses and houses with view 0. Which is strange as their high price would have led us to believe that they would have had either a nice view or a water source near the house.

  > As asked by **Point 5** we will try to see wether these high prices can be explaine dby other characteristics such as size `sqrt`) and `grade` which are the variables we analyzed before.

library(knitr)

num <- data[, sapply(data, is.numeric)]

##### Throwback to Part 4

We want to check whether the houses without a view or waterfront had other reasons for their high prices, despite lacking these features. Since there are many of them, we only examine the top 10.

The ten most expensive houses without waterfront and with view 0 are all large (2,800–4,800 sq ft) and have a high construction grade (9–12) and many bathrooms. Their high prices are therefore explained by size and quality rather than by view or waterfront,

## Task 2: Linear Regression

### Part 1

> Fit model M1: price \~ sqft_living and model M2: price \~ bedrooms, and plot each fitted regression line on the proper scatter plot. Which of the two models is better? Justify your answer. For the model you choose, interpret the coefficients, their significance, the 95% confidence intervals, the residual standard error (RSE) and the R2

As this assignemnt part is asking us tocomapre the performance of these two modxel, we feel the need to express how the first model will certainly be better than the second one, as the fitting of a linear regression in a categorical variable will have an extremely high probability to have worse performance thatn a continuos variable as sqft living

```{r}
M1 <- lm(price ~ sqft_living, data = data)
M2 <- lm(price ~ bedrooms, data = data)

# M1 model
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(data$sqft_living, data$price, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.3),
     xlab = "sqft_living", ylab = "Price", main = "M1: price ~ sqft_living")
abline(M1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

#M2 model
plot(data$bedrooms, data$price, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.3),
     xlab = "bedrooms", ylab = "Price", main = "M2: price ~ bedrooms")
abline(M2, col = "red", lwd = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

As expected M1 performs far better. 

#### Model choice: M1

Considering these results we choose M1 as our model. We will now interpret the coefficients, their significance, the 95% confidence intervals, the residual standard error (RSE) and the R2 as requested

```{r}
summary(M1)
confint(M1)
```

By looking at the summary and coefficient we can say:

- The **intercept** that predicts price at 0 sq ft, does not have any practical meaning. Any house with 0 ft living area cannot be defined as a house

- **β₁** tells us that each extra sq ft adds about 285 USD on average

- The **significance tes**t we made with p values tells us that both coefficients have p \< 0.001. For the slope, p \< 2e-16, so we **reject H₀: β₁ = 0.**

- The **95% CI for β₁:** [272, 298]. It’s narrow and doesn’t contain 0, which confirms the significance.

- **RSE = 270,400 USD:** the typical prediction error is large, so size alone gives only rough predictions.

- **R²:** `sqft_living` alone explains about 48% of the variability of price (R² = 0.48),

- **Residuals** are asymmetric (max +3.25M vs min −884k). The model underestimates very expensive houses which is consistent with the right skew of price.
